name: MindBridge OpenLane Basic Neural Mesh
description:
The MindBridge OpenLane is a no-frills cortical mesh implant designed for maximum accessibility at minimum cost. Installed via a single-session outpatient procedure at any licensed MindBridge clinic or partnered walk-in, the mesh spreads a thin lattice of biocompatible nanofibers across the prefrontal and parietal cortices, enabling basic feed access, AR overlay rendering at 720p equivalent, push-notification messaging, civic identity authentication, and QUANTA payment integration. Bandwidth is capped at 40 Mbps with a two-channel processing architecture — sufficient for everyday navigation, transit scheduling, employer check-ins, and government service access, though multitasking beyond two simultaneous applications causes noticeable lag.

The OpenLane is the single most common BCI in the Shelf and lower Tier 2 districts of GLMZ — some estimates place it in roughly one in three implanted skulls city-wide. For many residents, it is their first and only neural interface, often subsidized through city welfare programs or employer onboarding packages from logistics and service-sector corporations. Life with the OpenLane is functional but unglamorous: users grow accustomed to the half-second render delay on AR overlays, the occasional dropped feed connection in dense signal environments, and the mildly intrusive MindBridge advertisement watermark that appears in peripheral vision unless a monthly suppression fee of Φ12 is paid. It is the BCI equivalent of a prepaid phone — most people have one, nobody brags about it.
installation_requirements: Single outpatient session at any MindBridge licensed clinic or partnered walk-in facility; no specialist required; local anesthetic only
rejection_risk: Low — standard biocompatible nanofiber mesh with a well-documented 97.3% acceptance rate across diverse neurological profiles
maintenance: Automatic firmware updates pushed monthly via feed; annual recalibration recommended but not required; no hardware maintenance needed under normal use
specifications: {"bandwidth": "40 Mbps", "channels": 2, "ar_resolution": "720p equivalent", "encryption": "AES-128 civic standard", "battery": "Passive induction — no dedicated power cell", "latency": "18-35ms", "feed_protocols": ["CivNet", "MeshPublic", "QUANTA-Pay v3"], "smartlink": false, "update_method": "OTA automatic"}
side_effects: Mild tinnitus in the first 2-4 weeks post-installation during neural pathway formation
Peripheral AR ghosting during high-traffic signal zones (transit hubs, markets)
Occasional involuntary feed intrusion during REM sleep — advertising fragments reported by approximately 18% of users
Mild headaches during peak network congestion hours
cultural_context: The OpenLane carries a quiet social stigma in Tier 3 and above — recognizable by its slightly sluggish AR render and the telltale MindBridge watermark glow at the corner of users' eyes. In the Shelf, however, it is simply a fact of life, and many residents feel a pragmatic pride in having any BCI at all. Corporate recruiters in Tier 3 firms sometimes note OpenLane implants on applications as a subtle negative signal, shorthand for 'hasn't upgraded yet,' which has driven a small secondary market in cosmetic firmware skins that mimic the visual output signature of more prestigious brands.
known_users: first-time BCI recipients on city subsidy programs
undocumented migrants who acquire units second-hand
elderly Tier 2 residents who resisted implantation until civic services mandated it
story_hooks: A Shelf organizer discovers that the monthly 'ad suppression fee' charged by MindBridge is actually funding a data-harvesting operation selling behavioral profiles to Tier 5 corporate interests — and the OpenLane's passive architecture makes it nearly impossible to opt out.

A player character's OpenLane begins receiving fragmented transmissions that don't match any known feed protocol — someone is using the mesh's low-security architecture as a dead drop, and dangerous people want to know who has been receiving the signal.

A city welfare program is quietly discontinuing OpenLane subsidies, leaving thousands of Shelf residents facing loss of civic identity authentication — effectively making them legally invisible — unless someone can expose the corporate lobbying behind the decision.
